title: Older musicians who could not keep up; learning to read
summary: They discuss Quartell and Snyder aging out, Paul Mares quitting over reading, and the Wolverines' reaction to reading.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: It, uh, seems that music was changing rapidly enough that, uh, if you couldn't change with it, it might be left behind. Frankie Quartell says that he dropped out of music. He just couldn't keep up. And, uh, you would recognize him, of course, as an earlier generation, five or ten years of Columbia. And, and he never could quite, uh, rid himself of what was back up. Frank Snyder, uh, as a drummer, too, might have grown out of date. Well, now, uh, the new fellows coming up in Chicago, uh, those who, uh, grew to prominence in the mid-twenties, didn't seem to suffer that aging quite as severely, did they? No. I mean, Jimmy's still working today, but still working today.

No, they didn't. They had a condom. No, that's a, that's a, a funny thing. There, there are, of course, there are the old legends about what happened when the, when the necessity for learning to read came up. Uh, Paul Mayers, for instance, said any time he had to read what somebody else wrote for him, he'd quit. He said that's why he started the barbecue place on North State. Um, I can remember that, I think it was George Johnson and the Wolverines, when Dick Voino announced that everybody was going to have to learn to read, and Dick was the only one who did know how. There was that absolute dead silence, and, and, uh, Johnson said, what do we do if the lights go out? They'd been playing in two or three places where they'd been shot out, and that maybe had something to do with it. I think you're right that, that the, uh, well, the, the Austin boys didn't have much to change because they were pretty young, you see, and they were on top of the world in a way. This might interest you. When I took their record east to Princeton, the 26 record that they made, uh, and played it for musicians in Princeton, they thought I was out of my head.
